https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy.text: Oops, something went wrong U.S. markets closed Hungarian companies pivot after Orban’s allies lose political influence Simon Mugo August 2, 2026 2 min read APPB OPUSG IGNY Investing.com -- Hungarian companies associated with former Prime Minister Viktor Orban are scaling back large projects and reassessing their businesses after Péter Magyar's election victory ended Orban's 16-year rule, Reuters reported. Magyar's new government has pledged to tackle alleged favouritism in public procurement and review contracts awarded under the previous administration. Construction groups that relied heavily on state-funded infrastructure projects face the greatest risk as public tenders become more competitive. Market Epito, one of Hungary's largest construction companies, plans to shift from major developments towards a greater number of smaller housing and infrastructure projects. About one-quarter of its revenue has come from public contracts. The company is linked to Orban ally Istvan Garancsi but said its financial strength and diversified portfolio were not dependent on political cycles. Duna Aszfalt, Hungary's largest road-construction company, also said it was prepared to compete under the new system. Magyar's government has suspended an extension of a motorway in southern Hungary and asked Duna Aszfalt to repay funds received for the project before the election. Public procurement practices had faced scrutiny under Orban. A 2024 OECD survey found that Hungary had a high rate of tenders attracting only one bidder. Reforms designed to increase competition are among the European Union's conditions for releasing funding suspended over rule-of-law concerns. Parliament received broad anti-corruption legislation in June aimed at improving transparency in the use of public money. Shares of companies viewed as politically connected, including Opus Global, Appeninn, 4iG and MBH Bank, have fallen sharply as investors removed premiums associated with their previous influence. Those declines have contrasted with a broader rally in Budapest-listed stocks, supported by expectations that more transparent tenders could attract foreign investment. Analysts said some businesses built around preferential access to state contracts may not survive the transition. International companies could gain market share in construction, defence, telecommunications and media as contracts are reopened to wider competition. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-t.text: BRUSSELS — In Europe's fight against wildfires, eyes are turning toward the sky: not just looking for rain or water-dropping Canadair planes, but also for ways to exploit new satellite capabilities to help contain or even prevent new blazes. Satellites and the images and data they gather from space are increasingly seen as a means of providing European governments and firefighters on the ground with more accurate information: to map damage and detect fires at an early stage. Such help is more than welcome during another scorching European summer with wildfires in France, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Approximately 600,000 hectares have burned across EU countries since the start of the year. Just last weekend, Belgium was hit by one of the largest wildfires in its history, in the High Fens nature reserve. Advertisement Advertisement Still, this latest use of satellites is another reminder that Europe needs to step up its game in yet another strategic arena. After Elon Musk’s Starlink showed how satellite-based services could revolutionize everything from mobile communication to waging war, space technology for disaster management offers a potential avenue for Europe to compete. Greece, a country that seems to be battling bigger wildfires every summer, was the first to act. In early May, a rocket of Musk’s SpaceX carried four small satellites into space with the specific task of helping the country detect and track wildfires in near real time. It was a crucial step in the build-out of the “Hellenic Fire System,” which the Greek government boasted was the first national satellite system of its kind. The system was set up through European-wide collaboration, with the help of the European Space Agency, its Greek counterpart, German wildfire intelligence platform Ororatech and Finnish radar-based satellite provider ICEYE. “By integrating space-based capabilities into our emergency response systems, we are equipping our fire services with the tools they need to respond faster,” Dimitrios Papastergiou, Greece's minister of digital governance and artificial intelligence, said at the launch in May. The satellites that were launched before the summer were equipped with two infrared imagers. Those pick up the heat energy radiated by fires, allowing satellites to detect hotspots and gauge their intensity. Advertisement Advertisement The system is designed to “support early detection of emerging hotspots and continuous monitoring of fire behavior,” the European Space Agency said. Satellites' role in gathering vast, real-time data and images can also help with other extreme weather events. The Finnish company ICEYE offers monitoring services for governments and businesses to manage both natural catastrophes, such as floods and wildfires, and man-made ones, such as illegal deforestation. ICEYE raised €1 billion in new financing this year, and became the first company to get backing from the Scaleup Europe Fund, a new fund backed by the European Commission to help companies expand rapidly. “If we want to be effective in managing the environment around us, both in terms of growth and development, as well as preventing or managing natural catastrophes, these sorts of space-based systems are extremely effective,” ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski told POLITICO. He said the company has been mostly focused on “managing” wildfires, but is now “trying to push towards predicting wildfires or at least detecting them in an earlier stage.” Modrzewski says a similar offering is available for floods, and for wind damage stemming from hurricanes and typhoons. The impact can be maximized if Brussels becomes a coordinating “buyer” of those services. “Using space-based capabilities is much more effectively done on an EU scale through [the European] Commission than on a national scale in 27 separate nations,” Modrzewski said. The Commission is already prominent in helping governments and emergency services map and detect wildfires. The European Forest Fire Information System , which sits within the Commission’s research desk, maps both active fires and burned areas based on data from NASA's MODIS and the European Space Agency's Sentinel-3, an Earth observation satellite. Currently, data and images arrive every 10 minutes, but the launch of a new satellite from the Meteosat third generation next Thursday should speed that up — with images arriving every 2.5 minutes, improving detection and even forecasting of possible wildfires. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/riot-poli.text: Jakub Krupa Updated Sat, October 31, 2026 at 6:37 AM UTC 1 Police are seen around the premises of Poland's constitutional court after its head was suspended in Warsaw, Poland, on Friday.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status. The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy. The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court. The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time. Related: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain The PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, a close ally of Donald Trump, turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night. Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers. Shortly before 1am on Saturday, Nawrocki appeared outside the court and made his way through the police cordon , with one video showing the president tussling with security and other judges to force his entry into the building. As of 4am local time, the president remained inside the building. In a clip posted online , Nawrocki was heard saying the government appointees “were not judges of the constitutional court”. In a statement read out on his behalf outside the court at 5am, Nawrocki criticised “a violation of Poland’s constitutional order”, saying “a constitutional body was seized by force”. He called for security forces to leave the premises. The latest clash is likely to further polarise the country, setting the scene for a dramatic showdown in next year’s parliamentary election, with polls showing the populist-right with a chance to return to power. The court has been at the centre of a dispute dating back to 2015, when the outgoing centrist and the incoming rightwing governments moved in quick succession with legally questionable moves to stack the bench with their appointees. The dispute over the appointments paralysed the court , followed by further attempts to cripple it during the PiS’s eight years of illiberal rule marred by clashes with the EU over the rule of law. Since returning to power in 2023, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has repeatedly pledged to reverse controversial reforms as he sought to mend relations with Brussels , while refusing to recognise the court’s legitimacy in the current form. However, his efforts have been thwarted by opposition-aligned presidents who used their veto powers and expansive interpretations of their powers to block reforms. In the latest twist this year, Nawrocki, who unexpectedly won last year’s presidential election against Tusk’s candidate, refused to swear in five judges elected by the current parliament, further complicating the legal situation. Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission, said the president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts. On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary. Experts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”. Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work. Despite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.” “After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued. Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.” Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.” “What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said. Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move. US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.” “Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible.
